seoTitle: Set Up ATM-Style Trade Management in TradingView
metaDescription: See how to preset stop loss and take profit levels in TradingView's order ticket through a connected broker like Binance, similar to NinjaTrader's Advanced Trade Management.
intro: NinjaTrader traders coming to TradingView often go looking for an "ATM strategy" toggle and don't find one, because TradingView simply doesn't ship that feature by name. What it does have is a per-order Take Profit and Stop Loss section built into the trading panel itself, which, once your broker is connected, gives you almost the same outcome: a stop and a target attached to the trade before you ever click Buy. This guide shows where those fields actually live, what they look like filled in against a connected broker, and how to practice the workflow in a paper trading account before you risk real size.

steps.heading: Connect a broker that supports order-level risk management
steps.body: The bracket-style behavior you're after comes from your broker integration, not from TradingView's charting layer. Open the Trading Panel at the bottom of the chart and connect a supported account — Binance, OANDA, and TradeStation are common choices, and each surfaces the same Take Profit and Stop Loss fields once connected. The panel shows your account balance, equity, and open orders right next to the chart, so you can see risk exposure and price action in the same view instead of switching windows.

steps.heading: Open the order ticket and set your units
steps.body: Click into a Buy or Sell action to open the order ticket, which slides out over the right side of the chart. Start with Units — the size of the position — and TradingView calculates the margin and total order value live as you type. This ticket has three order types across the top, Market, Limit, and Stop, and the risk fields you're setting up next apply the same way regardless of which one you pick.

image.caption: The order ticket on a connected Binance account, with Units set and the Take Profit and Stop Loss checkboxes sitting just below the order type tabs.

steps.heading: Attach Take Profit and Stop Loss before you confirm
steps.body: Below the Units field are two checkboxes, Take Profit and Stop Loss, each expanding into its own set of inputs for ticks, price, or a USD or percentage value. Check both, fill in your target and your stop, and they submit as part of the same order — this is the actual mechanism that replicates NinjaTrader's ATM behavior inside TradingView, even without a feature carrying that name. Because the fields accept ticks, price, or percentage, you can standardize your risk-to-reward ratio across instruments that trade at very different price scales instead of recalculating it by hand each time.

steps.heading: Watch the order and balance update in the panel below the chart
steps.body: Once an order is working, the panel beneath the chart tracks it under Orders, alongside Account Balance, Equity, and unrealized profit — all updating in real time as price moves. This is also where you'd go to modify or cancel a bracket after it's live, if the market shifts and your original stop or target no longer makes sense. Keeping this panel visible while you trade means you're never guessing whether an order actually attached correctly.

image.caption: The panel below the chart showing a connected Binance account — Account Balance, Equity, and the Orders tab listing working trades.

steps.heading: Practice the setup in Paper Trading first
steps.body: TradingView's built-in Paper Trading account uses the exact same order ticket and the same Take Profit and Stop Loss checkboxes as a live broker connection, which makes it the obvious place to rehearse this workflow before committing real funds. Switch the account selector from your live broker to Paper Trading, and you'll get a simulated balance to trade against with identical mechanics — same fields, same bracket behavior, zero real risk while you get the habit of checking both boxes on every entry.

image.caption: The same order ticket switched to a Paper Trading account, with Take Profit and Stop Loss ready to configure against a simulated balance.

steps.heading: Standardize it with a default risk-to-reward ratio
steps.body: Once the mechanics are comfortable, decide on a risk-to-reward ratio you'll apply by default — 1:2 is a common starting point — and use it to set your stop and target distance on every trade rather than eyeballing levels in the moment. Consistency here matters more than any single trade's outcome, since it's what keeps your losses capped while your winners are sized to actually outweigh them over a run of trades.

steps.heading: Go further with Pine Script alerts
steps.body: For anyone who wants entries and exits to trigger automatically rather than manually clicking Buy each time, Pine Script alerts can layer custom logic on top of this manual bracket setup — firing a webhook or notification when your conditions are met so you can execute the same TP/SL pattern faster. That's a separate, more advanced step from the order ticket workflow above, but it builds directly on the same Take Profit and Stop Loss fields once you're ready to automate.

faq.question: Does TradingView have a built-in ATM strategy feature like NinjaTrader?
faq.answer: No. TradingView has no feature by that name, but the order ticket's Take Profit and Stop Loss checkboxes, available once you connect a supported broker, produce a very similar bracket-order outcome.

faq.question: Which brokers support this Take Profit / Stop Loss setup?
faq.answer: Binance, OANDA, and TradeStation are common connected brokers that surface the fields in the order ticket. Support and exact behavior can vary by broker, so check your specific connection.

faq.question: Can I test this without risking real money?
faq.answer: Yes. Switch the account selector to Paper Trading and you get the identical order ticket and TP/SL fields against a simulated balance, which is the safest way to build the habit before trading live.

faq.question: Can I set a default risk-to-reward ratio?
faq.answer: TradingView doesn't auto-calculate a saved ratio for you, but you can apply one manually every time you set your stop and target distance in the order ticket, keeping it consistent trade to trade.

faq.question: Can I automate entries and exits further?
faq.answer: Yes. Pine Script alerts can trigger notifications or webhooks based on your own conditions, layering automation on top of the manual Take Profit and Stop Loss setup described here.
